8. Atrium (b): detail of a preserved section of the cocciopesto floor of the room, dating back to the Republican age and therefore older than the marble furnishings rebuilt in the imperial age (impluvium, table, fountain basin). The place of the impluvium was emphasized by a meandering border and squares outlined in white tiles.  79 N60665
9. Atrium (b), N-E corner: only the plaster preparation layer is completed, which preserves the imprints of the trowel.   79 N51372

10. Room (c): wall N with simple decoration in the fourth style consisting of a plinth with a red background, "decorated" only by sprays obtained with the brush dipped in white and yellow, and a discoloured middle area.

11. Room (c): wall E with the rectangular window open to the street and the rectangular brick-lined recesses in which the wooden beams of the attic were housed, immediately above which a rectangular splayed window, covered with plaster, is visible. The decoration of the room on the ground floor is the same as that on the N wall (see previous fig.) and is also repeated on the other two walls.
12. Room (f): cocciopesto floor dating back to the Republican age, with geometric ornamentation (diamonds and squares adorned with crosses) outlined in black and white tesserae.

13. Room (f): the small size of the N wall has suggested, above the black plinth "adorned" with splashes of yellow and red, the adoption of a bipartite scheme: in the center of the white middle area there is a narrow compartment containing a candelabrum; the state of conservation of the painting does not allow us to distinguish whether the side panels contained vignettes; The upper area is also white, above which the remains of the fresco that adorned the room on the upper floor are visible. IV style.

14. Cubicle (g): detail of the cocciopesto floor with geometric ornamentation (concentric squares) outlined in white tiles, which can also be dated — like the other floors of the house — to the Republican age.

15. Cubicle (g), S wall: contemporary with the floor is the fresco of the second style, now almost completely vanished. The decoration of the middle area marked the two parts of the room, diversifying the colors of the orthostats (yellow in the alcove and purple in the antechamber).
16. Cubicle (g), wall W with remains of a fresco of the second style. 79 N51339

17. Cubicle (h): detail of the floor of the antechamber, in cocciopesto adorned with a dotted with crosses of white tesserae with a central black tile; The inner row of the border also alternates between white and black tiles, while the outer row consists of only white tiles. The ornamentation can be dated to the Republican age and is considered by Pernice (Pernice, pp. 79-80) to be typical of the II style. i 79 N51352

18. Cubicle (h), N wall: this cubicle also preserves the remains of frescoes in the second style. Above a red plinth, the middle zone has green and yellow orthostats; a pillar delimits the innermost part, intended for the bed (alcove, on the right of the photograph). The decoration is repeated on the other walls, which are also in a very poor state of preservation.
19. Left wing (i): cocciopesto floor adorned only with a sparse dotted with small white tesserae.
20. Left wing (i): wall E with the remains of a fresco of the second style present, in the same conditions of preservation, on the other walls.

21. Tablinum (k): "relic" of the cocciopesto floor with ornamentation outlined in white tesserae consisting of geometric ornaments and crosses of only white tesserae, like the outer edge; on the inner edge, on the other hand, black and white tiles alternate.
22. Tablinum (k): N wall with remains of a fresco of the III style (the large central aedicule can be glimpsed). '79 N51324

23. Room (i): reproduction of the cocciopesto floor, which had in the center a floral ornamentation outlined in black and white tesserae, now disappeared, dated by Pernice (cited in the bibl.) to the Republican age.

24. Room (o): wall E with the remains of frescoes assigned by Mau (Mau W, p. 425) to the initial phase of the III style, which he defined as "candelabra". In the center of the middle area is an aedicule with a purple background, on which a large sacred landscape was painted. 79 N60563
25. Room (0), wall E, central section: detail of the architectural landscape.

26. Triclinium (p): remains of the cocclopesto floor with ornamentation outlined in white tesserae, which takes up the typical motif of the Republican age of the crosses of four white tesserae with a central black tile, here however consisting of spaced tesserae. The ornamentation consisting of large elements (hexagons and diamonds) that uniformly cover the carpet suggests a dating to the Imperial age.  79 N51362

27. Triclinium (p), N wall, O section: red geometric plinth; middle area with yellow panels bordered by circled carpet edges and separated by architectural foreshortening on a red background; on the right is visible the twisted candelabrum that delimited the central panel (see fig. below). Some characteristics of the decoration (the simple geometric plinth and the large carpet borders) would suggest that the decoration should be dated to the initial phase of the fourth style (before the implantation of the fullonica?).

28. Triclinium (p), N wall, section E: red geometric plinth; middle area with central panel with a large red border bordered by twisted candelabra and yellow side panels separated by a red foreshortening; white upper area with architecture. In the central panel there was a painting with Narcissus (So, 591), in the two adjoining panels medallions, which had already vanished at the time of the excavation, in the extreme panels vignettes with cupids (So, 315 and 328). IV style.
29. Triclinium (p), S wall, section E with remains of a fresco of the fourth style; the central panel with a large red border depicted the Judgement of Paris (So, 562).
30. Triclinium (p), wall W with remains of a fresco of the fourth style; in the center of the middle area was a large painting (see fig. below). On the left you can see the walled door of the S wall.
31. Triclinium (p): the painting depicting Zeus and Hermaphrodite (So, 74) which was in the centre of the O wall, now lost, in a drawing by G. Discanno.

32. Peristyle (q): view from S-W with brick and opus mixtum columns covered with plaster, above which part of a small floor and a moulded cornice are preserved. In the foreground are the tanks related to the fullonica plant.

33. Peristyle (q): raised portico on the S side with the layout of the fullonica basins. The high plinth of cocciopesto relating to the planting of the fullonica was made before the frieze of the upper area was painted (So, 653), which must therefore be placed in relation to this phase.  AFS A171 (formerly A7318)

35. Peristyle (q), portico S, wall E, scene of judgment: in front of four male figures seated on a suggestive protected by a curtain, a male figure dressed in a white tunic with red bands and a male figure, naked and bleeding, are carried.
36. Peristyle (q), S portico, wall E: detail of fig. 35: the guard with the spear brings the two contenders before the judging panel.

37. Peristyle (q), S portico, S wall, section E: frieze with five male figures in an excited attitude and dressed in short tunics, depicted between a pillar adorned with bandages and a dipylon. The figuration must still be referred to the scene of judgment.
38. Peristyle (q), S portico, S wall, section E: detail of fig. previous. One of the heads bears the signs of an attempted theft.

39. Peristyle (q), S portico, S wall, section E: two quarrelling. The face of the figure on the left seems to have caricatured features. The frieze continues, very difficult to read, on the rest of the wall and on the corner section (S portico, W wall).

40. Room (r), with masonry basins leaning against the S wall. The cocciopesto floor, which in the anterior part of the room had an ornament outlined in white tesserae, containing a phallus, branches, two cornucopias and the inscription SALVE (now preserved only in plate 35, 4 of the Pernice and in fig. 68 of the Warsher) must have been made before the installation of the basins.
1. Room (c), N wall: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a red plinth, yellow middle area, white upper area with architecture and moulded stucco cornice.
2. Room (c), corner S-E: red plinth and yellow middle area with edges of staple carpet. IV style.

3. Room (d), N wall with simple decoration of the fourth style: above the red plinth, with panels with plants separated by narrow compartments, the middle area and the upper area are both white. The panels of the middle area are bordered by carpet edges and separated by narrow compartments crossed by taut garlands; the upper area contains architecture.
4. Room (d), detail of the previous figure: of the vignettes with animals that decorated the panels, only the griffin that adorned the central panel is preserved. IV style.
5. Room (d), N wall, section E: the remains, now illegible, of a vignette that perhaps showed a bird in flight with a ribbon in its beak.

6. Room (d), wall O with a bipartite scheme: red plinth with plants; white middle area with a central compartment crossed by twisted candelabra and white side panels bordered by carpet edges, which contained cartoons with animals in the center; white upper area. IV style.

7. Room (e): reproduction of the simple wall decoration, which takes up the colors and simple patterns attested in the room (d): above the red plinth with plants, the middle area and the upper area are both white (in this case, given the absolute simplicity of the decoration, this circumstance is certainly important). 14, 25

8. Room (e), N wall with remains of a fresco of the fourth style. The holes in the poles that supported the reed of the false vault follow the profile of the lunette, bordered by a simple stucco frame.
9. Room (e), wall E, central section: detail of the simple stucco frame.
10. Room (e), wall S: the current state of conservation of the decoration reproduced in fig. 7 allows us to verify the substantial accuracy of the nineteenth-century reproduction.
12. Room (e), detail of the previous figure: simple carpet edges outlined in red on the white background of the panel. 79 N54372
11. Room (e), O wall, S-shaped section of the window open onto the small viridarium (f): red plinth with panels and compartments with plants; white middle area. IV style.
14. Room (e), detail of the previous figure: in the compartment that divides the white panels of the middle area there is a golden twisted candelabrum, surmounted by the globe. IV style. 79 N54338
13. Room (e), wall W, section N with remains of fresco of the fourth style.

1. The old photograph documents the façade of no. 28, with the large door of the workshop (c) protected by a practicable canopy supported by wooden beams, housed in rectangular holes lined with bricks; the canopy gave access to the latrine, located in the niche at the S end of the upper floor.
2. The façade of no. 28, after the collapse of the upper floor, following the bombing of the Second World War.

3. Façade: detail of the tuff sign with terracotta edges on which two pairs of phalluses are carved as good luck charms, on either side of a case for the game of dice (fritillus, cf. Annecchino, cited in bibl.): the function of the object is demonstrated by the discovery of a jar of similar shape, containing a dice (P. Egidi in ArchCI, 35, 1983, pp. 283-286).

4. Workshop (c), wall N: the room had a rather accurate decoration of the fourth style; above the purple plinth, the white middle area had the aedicule in the center flanked by marsh reeds that supported garlands and separated from the side panels by complex architectural views crossed by candelabra and closed by partitions adorned with animal protomes within corollas. In the center of the middle area was a painting depicting Venus the Fisherress, in the side panels were vignettes (on the left depicting a cupid, on the right Dionysus and Hermes).

5. Workshop (c), wall N: the current condition of the wall documented by the old photograph reproduced in fig. previous. On the left is the door that gives access to house no. 30, through the atrium (a).

8. Workshop (c): the painting with Polyphemus and cupid that was in the center of the S wall, in a reproduction by G. Discanno.
10. Workshop (c), wall O, section S: detail of fig. with the tragic mask on a candelabrum painted on the purple plinth. IV style.  79 N60557
9. Workshop (c), wall O, section S: remains of fresco of the fourth style. In the center of this wall was the painting reproduced in fig. 11.  79 N60559
11. Workshop (c), wall O: painting with cupids with bunches of grapes (So, 181).
12. Sidewalk in front of the entrance to the house, at no. 30, in cocciopesto with scattered limestone flakes.
13. Vestibule (e), a floor of papier-mâché with dotted white tiles.

14. Atrium (a), wall S: the current state of the decoration reproduced in the following figures. Once the painting was detached, with a particularly interesting subject, the wall was abandoned to complete decay. 79 N60556 351

15. Atrium (a), S. The old photograph contemporary with the excavation and prior to the detachment of the central painting, together with the nineteenth-century descriptions and reproductions, makes it possible to reconstruct the original appearance of this decoration, now completely vanished (see fig. 14). The aedicule occupying the center of the middle area was surmounted by a yellow frieze with Egyptian figures (So, 490) and flanked by a yellow frieze with a yellow frieze with Egyptian figures.
16. Reproduction of the wall in fig. previous; cf. also fig. 17.

17. Atrium (a), S wall: painting depicting the death of Laocoön and his sons (So, 581; MNN inv. 111210). A painting with the same subject and the same iconography, inserted within a wall decoration scheme of a little later (IV style), comes from the wing of the House of Menander I 10,4 (cf. vol. II, p. 284, fig. 68). Beyen (cited in the bibl.) compares the painting with that of Palladio's rape from House I 2,6 (cf. vol. I, p. 15, fig. 18), in which the names of the protagonists are indicated by captions in Greek.

18. Cubicle (d): cocciopesto floor with ornamentation outlined in black and white tesserae; the motif that adorned the central carpet, bordered by a row of white tesserae, is now lost; a row of meanders outlined in white tesserae, with black tesserae at the edges, forms its edge. The drafting of the floor decoration, which can still be dated to the Republican age (II style), is prior to the detachment of the room (d) from the house and the opening of the independent entrance at no. 29, as can be seen from the motif of the threshold that emphasized the original access to the atrium (a), which can be glimpsed under the infill of the door.

19. Cubicle (d): N wall with late III style decoration. The black plinth is surmounted by a middle area with a large central aedicule with a red background and black side panels, separated by architectural views; in the center of the wall is the large gash left by the detachment of the painting with a female figure on a bed (see fig. below). The painting helps to define the era of the detachment of the cubicle from the house, which took place after the execution of the decoration itself and therefore in the years following the middle of the first century AD; on that occasion the other walls were covered with cocciopesto, which follows the course of the staircase now leaning against the S wall and covers the infill of the door on the O wall, through which one passed from the atrium to the cubicle.
20. Cubicle (d): reproduction of the wall shown in fig. in the centre of which is the painting with Aphrodite the Fisher from workshop no. 28 (see fig. 4).

21. The painting from the N wall of the cubicle (d) (So, 641; MNN inv. 111209) depicts a couple feasting on the kline within a room overlooking a peristyle; on the left, a standing female figure addresses the couple (caught "in the act"?), accompanied by a slave holding a tablet in his right hand.

27. Room (n), wall O: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a black plinth and a yellow middle area with the edges of a semicircular carpet.

26. Room (m), N wall with remains of a fresco of the III style: the plinth was black, the middle area has a yellow central panel with a high red border and a red side panel crossed by a thin candelabrum. On the wall were painted two figures, already damaged at the time of the excavation and now completely disappeared, an Apollo or a Muse from Liricine, and a smaller female figure (So, 646). The decoration was evidently carried out in a phase in which the room, annexed to the bakery in the last phase of the house, had a different purpose, probably tricliniary.

29. Bakery (p), S wall with remains of a fresco with a black background (panels bordered by red bands). 79 N60565

1. Façade with opus incertum masonry and cubic tuff capitals, dating back to the Republican age. The façade and the E wall of the vestibule (1) are covered with rough plaster, with raised pilasters that frame both the entrance door to the house and the passage from the vestibule to the atrium.
2. Atrium (2), O wall, N section with plinth with simple orthostats.

3. Triclinium (c), S-E corner with recess for the bed and remains of a fresco (black plinth and white middle area) datable according to Mau (cited in bibl.) to the III style. According to Pernice (cited in the bibl.), the floor had a rectangular "mat" formed by eighty marble slabs, perhaps executed at the same time as the wall decoration. In this room a "treasure" of 347 imperial coins was found (NSc 1877, pp. 221-222; cf. L. Breglia, in Pompeiana, p. 58, table B, no. 35). 79 N60599
1. Workshop (a), overall view from O. AFS C1292

2. Workshop (a), wall N: above the masonry in opus incertum with ample relief in mixed techniques were painted the scenes reproduced in figs. 4-6. The amphorae and the dolio were intended to contain wine.

3. Bottega (a), S-W corner with the masonry serving counter, overlooking the alley through a large opening with jambs in blocks of square limestone and tuff. In the counter, which at the time of the excavation was covered with plaster painted with faux marble, there are two dolii.

4. Workshop (a). Standing couple embracing, near which the phrase "nolo/Myrtale" is painted. The meaning of the scene, despite the inscription, is unclear, as it is not possible to distinguish whether they are male or female figures. AFSN C4249

5. Bottega (a): second scene: on the left two seated patrons, approached by a female figure (?) carrying a tall glass. The dialogues seem to refer to problems of "precedence" in the service: the figure on the left calls towards him (hoc); the one in the center contrasts the desire of the first patron (non/ mia est), the impatient "maid" replies qui vol/sumat (take it whoever wants), while inviting a third unrepresented character (Oceane/ veni bibe) to drink. AFSN C4206

6. Bottega (a): in the third scene two players are depicted seated at a table: the one on the left holds the cartridge case or fritillus (the same object depicted in the sign of the nearby workshop no. 28: cf. p. 343, fig. 3) and believes he has won (exsi), the one on the right contests the result (non / tria duas/ est).

1. Atrium (b), corner N-E with remains of plaster on the ground floor and on the upper floor. On the left is the N wall of the wing (d) (see fig. 5): fig. Warsher 142, on which one can still easily follow Mau's description (Mau BdI 1878, pp. 187-188), attests to a much better state of preservation.
2. Atrium (b), wall E with the remains of a simple covering consisting of a high red plinth surmounted by a unitary white area, which Mau attributed to the III style (Mau BdI 1878, p. 187).
3. Triclinium (c), central section S wall, with the remains of a painted shell.  79 N60609
4. Triclinium (c), wall O: imitation marble plinth (motif extraneous to the repertoire of the IIIl style) and middle area with a central aedicule with a blue background. 79 N60595

5. Wing (d), wall E with remains of a fresco of the III style; above the white plinth with plants ("unusual color and bad taste": Mau BdI 1878, p. 187), the middle area had a painting with a sacred landscape in the center within the aedicule, the side panels were red. III style.

1. Cubicle (d), wall N. Unlike what happened in the cubicle (c), located on the other side of the vestibule, in this room the oldest decoration of the first style has been maintained, although it has been renewed where necessary. It consists of a plinth surmounted by a low relief plan; of the original decoration of the middle area, only two rows of low polychrome ashlars are preserved, whose profiles were further emphasized by white raised strips; above the dentilled cornice the

2. Cubicle (d), wall E: the decoration is the same as on wall N, but the large original orthostat of the middle area is also preserved; the alcove is also ended laterally by a pilaster, at the door. The remains of plaster preserved in the upper area of the wall, above the dentilled cornice, in an area that, in the walls of the first style, is normally left to rough plaster, refer to the information of Mau (Mau W, p. 88), according to which orthostats and vanished figures were painted here.

3. Cubicle (d), wall O: the photograph includes the two parts in which the decoration in the first style of the room is structured, which distinguishes the antechamber on the left and the alcove on the right, separated by a low pilaster, in a position corresponding to the one that, on the wall in front, also acts as a jamb (see previous fig.).

4. Triclinium (e), N wall, section O: black geometric plinth, red middle area, black frieze, white middle area. The indication of the colors, illegible today, is taken from the Mau (Mau W, pp. 397-399), which also provides an accurate (and very "sympathetic") description of the individual decorative elements of the wall, which ensured its dating to the initial phase of the III style.
5. Triclinium (e), wall E, section N with remains of a fresco of the III style (black plinth and red middle area), which contained a painting with landscape in the center.

6. Triclinium (e), S wall, section O: in the central aedicule we can recognize the "shadow" of the painting with Pindar and Corinna (see fig. below), above which was a painting with instrumentum scriptorium. III style.

7. Triclinium (e). The painting with Pindar, Corinna and Myrtis (So, 644) in a drawing by DAIR (cf. the painting with the same subject, but limited to the two most famous protagonists, from Casa I 4, 5.25, vol. I, pp. 161162, figs. 71-72).

8. Triclinium (e), wall O: in the aedicule in the center of the red middle area there was a small picture with a landscape, above which, in the upper white area, there was a small picture with a rooster and a basket of fruit. III style.

9. Room (f), wall E: below a restoration with a black plinth and a middle area with a red central panel and yellow side panels, probably datable to the fourth style, a raised floor dating back to the first style can be seen in the upper area of the wall.

10. Triclinium (1): of the decoration of this room only the reproduction of the painting with Theseus and Ariadne (So, 526; the drawing is by G. Discanno) is preserved, for which Mau (Mau W, p. 427) recalled the painting with the same subject of the House of Neptune VI 5,3 (cf. vol. IV, p. 304, fig. 11). This comparison, and the description made by the same author in BdI 1878, p. 118, suggest that this decoration should be dated to the transition phase between the III and IV styles. The archaeological evidence of the seriousness of this phase compared to that of the III style attested in the rest of the house is given by the walled door on the E wall of the room, after the decoration of the peristyle had been carried out, but before the execution of that of the triclinium itself.
11. Room (o), N wall: yellow plinth moved only by polychrome "sprays"; middle area with red and yellow panels. The same decoration is repeated on the other walls.

12. Exedra (q), N-W angle: yellow plinth with plants and red middle area. The decoration of the room was rather simple and contained only, in the red and black panels of the middle area, vignettes with birds, cupids and a sphinx (Mau BdI 1878, pp. 117-118; contra Warsher, no. 158). IV style.

13. Exedra (q), S wall, section E: yellow plinth with plants, low white frieze with lotuses and middle area with red and black panels separated by a narrow yellow compartment with a stretched garland. IV style. 79 N60616

1. Atrium (b), view from N-W in an old photograph. On the side of the impluvium opposite the vestibule (a) is the marble table resting on two low masonry supports painted red (now removed): the trapezoids in the shape of an animal paw are adorned with winged griffin protomes, behind which are compartments with cornucopias and palms. In the background, leaning against the S wall, were column drums, fluted and covered with stucco, which according to Mau (Mau BdI 1878, p. 87) supported 386

2. Atrium (b): at the bottom of the cocciopesto impluvium there is a motif outlined in white tiles: a rose window of rhombuses is bordered by a border with meanders alternating with squares, and in the resulting fields there are four corner palmettes (cf. in this same insu/a the adjacent house no. 40, fig. 5, p. 393). The ornamentation, datable to the first style, was subsequently surrounded by a papier-mâché floor which, around the impluvium, bears a border bordered by a row of white tesserae densely juxtaposed by a dotted polychrome rectangular tesserae arranged in a basket. On the W side, facing the vestibule, in white tesserae, is outlined one of the few floor inscriptions of greeting and good wishes preserved (lucrum gaudium: CIL X, 875). This reconstruction can still be dated within the Republican age (II style).

The appearance of the god is decidedly oriental with a Phrygian cap, long robe, high shoes and strongly tanned complexion, long beard, gold necklace, bracelets and earrings to accentuate the character of opulence evoked by his figure and invoked for the inhabitants of the house. The absence of preparations to support the offerings excludes that the painting could have had a sacred character, while its placement towards the entrance emphasizes its apotropaic function. The position of the figure is the same as that of the Satyr present in one of the panels of the peristyle, probably derived from a model of the fourth century BC modified in Priapus with the accentuation of oriental characters, the addition of clothes and the replacement of the syringe held in the right hand with the scales.

The young hunter, loved by Apollo represented by the Delphic tripod, weeps sadly abandoned and turned towards his favorite deer, which he has wounded to death by mistake. The animal, although fully developed, as indicated by the branching horns, is smaller than the size of the picture would require. 33. Oecus (e), S wall: detail of the central aedicule in the upper area with Leda enthroned. The figure certainly derives from a type adopted for depictions of Venus, which draws its origins from the painting of the Anadiomène of Apelles exhibited in the Temple of Divus Julius in Rome and recurring several times in Pompeian paintings with representations of the goddess with Mars. The swan has obviously been added to the figure to characterize the heroine who, together with Danae and a third unidentified woman present on the E wall, is one of the many mortals loved by Zeus, recognizable on the O wall, parents of heroes or royal lineages. The representation of Leda seated, which was found in Pompeii again in IX 2, 7, does not have its origins in the original sculpture by Timotheos who depicted her standing, and to whom, known through numerous replicas in marble and terracotta or in representations in other materials (goldsmiths, ivories), the painters of other compositions (House of Queen Margherita V 2,1; House of the Ancient Hunt, VII 4,48). The predella was adorned with griffins ending in volutes, facing a schematic protome of a feline with a ring in its jaws.

108. Triclinium (n): the painting in the center of wall E has as its subject the killing of Pentheus. The nephew of Cadmus, whose name already foreshadowed a destiny of suffering, according to the Euripidean version of the myth, already known in a lost Pentheus by Aeschylus, had opposed the introduction of the cult of Dionysus that the god himself, accompanied by a thyasus of Lydian Maenads, was spreading in Thebes. He had tried in every way to stop their triumphant advance and to bring women to reason; incredulous even in the face of the wonders worked by the god, to spy on the mystery rites he goes to Cithaeron disguised as a bacchante and there Dionysus himself abandons him to the mystical fury of the women who tear him apart. Among them there is also Agave, her mother and Semele's sister who, condemned to madness for not having believed in the divinity of her nephew, will carry the severed head of her son as a trophy on the thyrsus. In another version, accepted by the painter of this painting, the young hunter king, armed with a spit and pole, becomes prey and victim. In fact, we find him, among the rocks of a wooded environment, surprised by three Maenads, two of which grab him by the hair and arms, forcing him to leave the spit, to hit him with the thyrsus while a third, behind him, is about to throw a heavy boulder at him. The group, despite the excitement of the movements of the characters, which fully conveys the idea of the tearing to which Pentheus will be subjected, has a closed circular pattern to which the two figures of Avttai with the chiton crossed on his chest, the torch in one hand and the whip in the other serve as a vertical reference.

'Triclinio (p): it is certainly the most sumptuous room in the house due to the structural characteristics of the decoration, the variety of ornamental elements and the rich polychromy that characterizes all its parts from the plinth, to the upper area in which aedicules and pavilions are arranged against the white background with the articulation of a theatrical scenography. On a plinth of cipollino, rectangular slabs of pavonazzetto (white and purple), serpentine (green) and numidic (yellow and red) alternate with squares containing medallions, in which, depending on the walls, the red granite is the background to roundels of numidic or vice versa. Aedicules that are not particularly deep but with coffered ceilings supported by precious metal columns in which the shoots alternate with groups of gigantomachies, host paintings with mythical stories linked by the theme of love. Two with a tragic conclusion because the object of love was "forbidden", the bull in the case of Pasiphae, Hera in that of Ixion and a third instead with a happy ending, the one between Dionysus and Ariadne. Contrary to what can be seen in the triclinium (n) in which the culminating moment and full dramatic action of the three episodes is represented, in this environment the painter quas1 shies away from representing the action, the myths are not grasped in the final phase, and also for that of Ixion in which the punishment is about to be inflicted on the transgressor,  the scene is dominated by the other protagonists so that the torture is barely glimpsed. Asymmetrical architectural views oriented towards the center of the wall flank the aedicules and are closed at the bottom by blue partitions that bear in the center, in relief, sea horses or busts of Minerva emerging from a corolla. On the walls, long panels with a white background framed by vegetable candelabras and garlands, restore the function of a diaphragm to the wall, absent in the aedicule and in the foreshortenings precisely because of the changing colors used in the backgrounds and decorative details. More than the complex frame of large and plastic lotus flowers, the small pictures with marine thjasoi or cupids, which close the aedicules and pavilions at the bottom with figures of offerers and divinities placed in a large complex room, whose structures curve at the bottom into an airy apse loggia, mark a precise caesura between the middle and the upper area. Triclinium (p): in the center of the wall E there is 11 painting with the myth of Ixion, the arrogant king of the Lapiths who, purified by Zeus and made immortal by him despite having killed his father-in-law, welcomed into Olympus undermined Hera; this, however, monogamous and faithful bride, revealed it to Zeus who with a cloud modeled an image with which Ixion united generating the Centaurs. The wrath of Zeus then punished the culprit for both crimes and Ixion was tied to a fiery wheel that would turn eternally while he repeated "You owe gratitude to your benefactor". An older version of the myth established that the punishment would take place in the sky; the presence of Hermes with petasus, caduceus and winged shoes, as well as that of the cloaked figure seated at his side, perhaps a deceased, indicate instead the setting in the Underworld. Hera, with the simple and austere diadem that is characteristic of her and the sceptre, a sign of her sovereignty, smugly witnesses the scene indicated to her by Iris standing at her side. Of Ixion, already tied to the wheel supported by Hephaestus, only part of the torso can be seen. The protagonists of this picture are the just and vengeful gods rather than the mortal who has not been able to deserve the trust of the father of the Olympians. Here too there is no lack of notation of an everyday nature in the representation of anvil, hammer and pincers, at the bottom left, almost a signature of the same artist of the painting with Daedalus and Pasiphae.

133-134. Room (q), N wall, central section: in the frieze scenes of the grape harvest are repeated at the ends and that of the pressing in the centre. Better preserved is the left end in which five cupids are intent on harvesting grapes from shoots stretched between trees, according to a cultivation technique described by Columella (Rei rust., IV, 30), Varro (De re rust., I, 8, 2) and Pliny the Elder (Nat. hist., XIV, 3,10 and 13; XVII, 35, 199). Two of them have climbed the branches themselves, one tries to lift a long ladder, a fourth has climbed on an upside-down basket and the fifth pours the bunches of grapes from a kàlathos into a larger basket. On the right follows the representation of the press for crushing the pomace, perhaps recognizable in the whitish spot at the bottom in the foreground. Two cupids are tightening the screw that lowers the prelum, inserting the long rods into the holes on the screw itself, and with great naturalness the physical effort of the small beings engaged in a task is made disproportionate to their possibilities. The group of a cupid holding a basket with an arched handle with his left hand and holding something with his right hand to a seated figure, not better identifiable who seems to be carrying a cup or an instrument to his lips, marks the separation with the continuation of the harvest scene (see fig. 132) in which we see a cupid bent over a large container to pour his collection into it,  one who harvests while standing on an overturned basket and one who carries a full basket. The composition of the scenes of these friezes is certainly of Hellenistic origin, but the immediacy of their rendering and the variety of details within the same theme is also the result of the familiarity of the scenes themselves, taken from the most widespread activities of the Pompeians.
